props.title: Bus 174
props.initialSlug: True story of a Rio bus hijacking gone tragically wrong

sections.content: Bus 174 revolutionized documentary filmmaking by merging real-time news footage with investigative journalism to create a haunting portrait of Brazil's social inequality. Director José Padilha masterfully weaves together the live television coverage of a Rio de Janeiro bus hijacking with deep exploration of hijacker Sandro do Nascimento's tragic backstory. The film's approach influenced later works like The Bridge (2006) and Senna (2010), showing how archival footage could be transformed into gripping narrative cinema. Padilha would later apply these documentary techniques to his narrative films, including Elite Squad (2007).

sections.content: The film's examination of systemic poverty and police violence resonates with other powerful Latin American documentaries like La Sierra (2005) and Cartel Land (2015). What sets Bus 174 apart is its real-time urgency combined with methodical investigation. Padilha shows how media coverage shaped public perception of the event while simultaneously deconstructing those same narratives through careful research and interviews.

The influence of Bus 174's hybrid storytelling approach can be seen in later works like The Imposter (2012) and Tower (2016), which similarly blend archival footage with investigative elements. These films demonstrate how documentary can serve both as immediate witness and thoughtful social commentary, particularly when examining traumatic public events. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Documentary Filmmaking

Bus 174's innovative use of multiple perspectives and timeline manipulation influenced a wave of documentaries about public crimes and media spectacle, including Dear Zachary (2008) and The Seven Five (2014). The film's ability to maintain suspense while delivering social commentary created a template for issue-driven documentaries that avoid becoming mere polemic.
